author: Awonusi Ayomide Jesudamilare
title: The Grid Inside the Grid
content:
In March, when 

Cassava Technologies announced the launch of an AI factory powered by NVIDIA

 in South Africa, the company described it as a turning point. African businesses would gain local access to high-performance computing. Data would remain within African borders. Developers would be able to build models for local languages and local problems.




The promise matters. African researchers and firms cannot participate meaningfully in artificial intelligence if they must rent every unit of computing power from servers abroad. But the most consequential infrastructure inside an AI factory may not be the graphics processor. It may be the electricity connection.




Artificial intelligence is exceptionally energy hungry. The 

International Energy Agency expects global electricity consumption by data centers to nearly double by 2030

. The pressure is not evenly distributed. Data centers cluster in particular cities and industrial corridors, where their demand can collide with already constrained transmission systems.




South Africa shows how this collision is being managed. Data center operators are increasingly securing electricity through private renewable plants and wheeling arrangements, which allow power generated in one province to travel across the national network to a customer elsewhere. author: Njeri Wangarĩ
title: The Fallacy that is the CBE Arts Pathway
content:
“So CBC is designed for short-term training of workers. In Europe, it is used among refugee and immigrant communities who need to be integrated into the community as fast as possible with skills they can use to earn a living. In other words, the adults are assumed to have basic human abilities of cultural identity, values, communication, and social skills, and all CBC is doing is giving workers tools for the workplace.” ~ 

Dr Wandia Njoya 




When Hannah*, our firstborn daughter, sat for her KJSEA exams last year, she was among the thousands of pioneers transitioning to Grade 10 in the newly established Kenyan Education Competency-Based Curriculum (CBC), since rebranded to Competency-Based Education (CBE).




Like many parents, I was drunk on the PR and the political rhetoric 

strungi

 that extolled the new curriculum above the 8-4-4 system, which we – a millennial generation still grappling with the side effects of exams, cramming, the Big 4 career options – blamed for our miserable lives stuck in jobs we hate but can’t quit. Not in this Kasongo economy.




We, the products of a system we felt seemed hell-bent on judging a fish based on its ability to climb a tree, together with the Ministry of Education, wanted to do away with exams completely. We had also swallowed the “talent carrot” that was dangled in front of us, whose hook – careers beyond being a doctor, lawyer,

author: Olive Kobusingye
title: Medical Ethics and the State’s Security Interests
content:
I grew up on a staple of detective novels. Agatha Christie, Ian Fleming, P.D. James, Colin Dexter… there was always the smart forensics team that ultimately cracked the case. The dried blood stain nobody had noticed, the single hair on the comb, the fingerprints on the backdoor doorknob… I wanted to become a forensics expert when I grew up. Either that, or a psychiatrist. There was something fascinating about being able to read people’s minds, and to set them right if they were disturbed. I carried these thoughts with me into medical school.




The psychiatrist option suffered a rude jolt during the three weeks I spent on the psychiatry rotation as a junior clerk. It seemed as though the patients never got well. Most patients we met had been there before, several times. There were three, at most four, drugs that were used to treat all conditions. And then there was the electroconvulsive therapy, which left me persuaded that I did not want to return to that unit if I had the choice. I am glad things have changed tremendously since.




I went into internship with an open mind. Two weeks in, I was told I was on medico-legal duty. The assigned doctor did post-mortems and could be called upon to examine inmates at the municipal prison. These were usually convicts whose sentences included corporal punishment – caning. Thankfully, it has been outlawed as a form of punishment.

author: Joshua W.J. Brown
title: The New Native Needs a Theory of Obligation, Not a Blood Test
content:
The New Native should not become the old Native with a better genealogy.




That is the danger I keep hearing underneath the question 

The Elephant

 has been asking this year. The “New Native” in this series is not a newly discovered ethnic group. It is a political figure emerging from a Kenyan public that has begun to act as though citizenship might mean more than being represented upward by an ethnic kingpin, disciplined by a church, managed by a civil servant, or frightened back into the inherited categories of the colonial state.




Akal Mohan sees the consolidation of a Kenyan identity beyond old orders of tribe, clan and denomination. Wangui Kimari traces the state’s fear of the “detribalized native”, then and now: the urban African who does not stay where authority says identity belongs. Joe Kobuthi reads the 2024 rupture through theology and the failure of a state that has demanded something close to sacred obedience. Across the series, the New Native becomes legible precisely when older intermediaries stop being able to explain the citizen to himself.




But once “native” is liberated from colonial administration, a second problem arrives. What is it going to mean?




If native means only ancestry, the term can become a blood test. If it means only citizenship, it can become historical amnesia. Neither answer is adequate for a country in which people can be equal

author: Akoko Akech
title: Homa Bay: The Road to Afgoonistan and the Van-goons of Democracy
content:
The political violence that characterized Linda Mwananchi’s forceful entry into Homa Bay and earned the county online mimetic mockery and nicknames such as Afgoonistan or Yemen didn’t begin in either the dust bowls of its lakeside town of Nyandiwa or the dusty roads of the county’s Ruma National Park, the route that the Linda Mwananchi entourage took to the heart of Homa Bay County, Asego ka DC, the administrative headquarters. 




It began in India with the intestate death of Raila Odinga. For over two decades, Raila’s charismatic leadership and competitive presidential ambition singularly disciplined both leaders and voters in Nyanza. Although it was the magnet that attracted disciplined ideologues, crass opportunists, and fellow travellers in Nyanza’s politics, it held competing egos and political ambitions in check. It also maintained a delicate balance within ODM: the contradictory or opposed politics of protest against the powers that be and the politics of protecting the powers that be, as the case may be, as well as the Luo elite politics of righting the wrongs of Kenya’s postcolonial state primarily as a national common good and only secondarily as a particular Luo ethnic good.    




Raila is dead. It is the end of an epoch. A new leadership struggles to be born in his Nyanza strongholds. Now it is time for monsters: castration angst, misogyny, sexism, mythical hist

author: Xinhu
title: The Reserve
content:
Cheng Huaijin stood before the enormous floor-to-ceiling window, swirling the South African red wine in her glass and admiring Mount Kilimanjaro in the distance under the clear sky. When she had moved into this office two years ago, she heard that seeing the snowcap of the mountain was a sign of good luck. Over these two years, the number of times she had received this “good luck” increased day by day, which made her firmly believe that she and Moshi city at the foot of the mountain were becoming luckier and luckier.




The city of Moshi, historically, was a trading center for the nearby farmers, herders, and merchants. Later, it became the gateway for foreign conquerors and climbers in the name of conquest to enter the Kilimanjaro region. Its long-standing agriculture, modestly successful light industry, and tourism had earned it a reputation for prosperity and tranquility in Tanzania. On the world stage, it remained an obscure city, until 2045, five years after enhanced robots spread across the globe. It was then that East Africa’s first Human Art Protection Reserve was established in Moshi. 




In an instant, this small city slumbering in the cradle of the highest mountain on the equator became a byword for fashion, modernity, and human dignity. Countless human tourists flocked here, just to leave a trace of their existence as humans in a dramatically altered world.

author: Yohannes Woldemariam
title: Imperial Nostalgia: History, Sovereignty, and the Unfinished Work of Decolonization in the Horn of Africa
content:
History in the Horn of Africa is rarely allowed to remain history. An ancient civilization becomes evidence of modern sovereignty. A medieval dynasty becomes proof of national continuity. Territory incorporated during one political era is later remembered as though it had always belonged to the state that governed it.




This habit has become especially visible as the Red Sea has returned to Ethiopian political discourse. Ethiopia is landlocked and has obvious economic reasons to seek dependable maritime trade. But there is a fundamental difference between negotiating the use of a port and claiming that a neighboring country possesses territory that properly belongs to Ethiopia. That distinction disappears when Assab is described as a “lost Ethiopian port.”




Ethiopia did not lose a sovereign port in 1993. Eritrea recovered sovereignty over territory that had been incorporated into Ethiopia after the violation and eventual termination of an internationally established federal arrangement. To describe this as Ethiopia “losing the sea” begins the story at the moment of Ethiopian possession and ignores how that possession came about.




This is what I mean by imperial nostalgia.




Imperial nostalgia is not merely admiration for emperors or attachment to an earlier age. It is a way of remembering political space. Territory once incorporated into an empire is remembered not si

author: Tafahri Munjatta
title: The World Was Never Mapped Innocently
content:
“A map is never neutral. It shapes perceptions and influences how people and continents understand their place in the world.” ~ Robert Dussey, Foreign Minister of Togo




The picture we inherit




There is a particular kind of silence that lives inside a classroom map.




It hangs above the blackboard, usually framed in plastic or pinned beneath glass. Countries sit in their familiar colours. Rivers thread across borders. Oceans stretch into blue emptiness. Africa occupies its assigned place, recognizable enough that few children think to ask who decided that this was what the world should look like.




The map appears to be showing us the world.




It is also teaching us how to see it.




This essay begins in a classroom, but something happened in a conference room in New York that makes the classroom worth reconsidering.




On September 4, 2026, the United Nations General Assembly endorsed a resolution encouraging the use of equal-area world maps, particularly the Equal Earth projection, in educational and media contexts. The vote was overwhelming: 164 countries supported it, the United States voted against it, and six abstained. The initiative was led by Togo with backing from the African Union. The resolution is non-binding. It does not outlaw the Mercator projection, redraw national borders, or declare one map universally correct. It asks institutions to reconsider

author: Frenny Jowi
title: Congo in Kenya: Why Xenophobia is a Racist Ideal
content:
Thirty-three-year-old Emmanuel is a freelance hairdresser in Nairobi. He is a refugee from the Democratic Republic of Congo and has lived in Kenya for six years.




The young man is chic, dressed in designer brands, with a gentle demeanour that reflects his customer-care style in the city’s beauty industry. His calm, collected appearance belies a history of strife, struggle, and an ongoing effort to recover from the decades of armed conflict he witnessed as a child in North Kivu.




‘I will never forget the night when rebels attacked our village in North Kivu. I must have been seven years old at that time. Some people were killed, and there was fire burning everywhere around us.’




Emmanuel narrated his story as he swung around in his styling chair in front of a large mirror that is popularly called a ‘station’ in Nairobi’s hairdressing and beauty salons.




I had visited Emmanuel at the salon where he works. Renting business premises in Nairobi is a significant cost for many young business owners, whether citizen or foreigner. In the beauty industry, most professionals can only afford to rent a mirror and a styling chair as a workstation – hence the name ‘station’.




While occasionally glancing at his WhatsApp notifications for customer bookings, Emmanuel continued to share his story with me.

author: Imani Verga
title: Chopsticks and Chapati: A Dar es Salaam Mosaic
content:
Preface




As new strangers walk old streets in the shade of mango and frangipani trees, something subtle stirs. Between chopsticks and chapati, “the Middle Kingdom” folds itself into “the Land of Kilimanjaro” both visibly and invisibly. Each story in this collection is a fragment of an unfolding quiet revolution lived not through the headlines, but through bubbling basins, bazaar booths, bodabodas, and blended babel. Here, at Tanzania’s “House of Peace” globalization settles in slowly through the rituals of eating, bargaining, commuting, and socializing. This is Dar es Salaam as it breathes today: a mosaic of memory, migration, and the delicate, daily negotiations of identity.




1: The Gate at Mayfair Plaza




Lemuani has manned the gate at Mayfair Plaza for almost seven years. Rain or shine, dust storms or downpours, he sits on a stool just inside the security booth, a navy blue uniform neatly pressed, his boots always polished, a thermos of chai keeping him company through the long shifts. The gate is both an entrance and a barrier, a place where class, race, and money collide in quiet, unspoken ways. To most who pass, he’s part of the scenery: a nod of acknowledgment, a raised barrier, a wave of the hand. But from where Lemuani sits, the gate is more than just a checkpoint. It is a stage, and he is both a sentry and silent witness to the daily theater of global exchange

author: Monica Atieno, Angela Chukunzira and Athandiwe Saba
title: Inside Kenya’s Hidden Deals with Big Tech
content:
When an outsourcing company working for Meta found itself being sued in Kenya, it took its problem to the President.




The dispute had begun in May 2022, when former Facebook content moderator Daniel Motaung sued Sama and Meta over working conditions. Another 43 moderators brought a case in March 2023. The workers had been employed by Sama to moderate Facebook content, work that required them to repeatedly view disturbing material. They argued that Meta, which ultimately benefited from and controlled aspects of their work, should also be held responsible.




Sama was not a minor contractor in Kenya. It was part of the labour pipeline that allowed a global technology company to outsource some of the most harmful work of the internet to Kenyan workers. Meta fought to remove itself from the litigation, arguing, among other things, that Kenyan courts did not have jurisdiction over the foreign company. But on 20 September 2024, the Court of Appeal rejected that argument.




Then on 11 November 2024, less than two months after that ruling, the Business Laws (Amendment) Bill was published. It proposed new rules for Kenya’s outsourcing industry, including provisions dealing with who should carry responsibility for workers employed by outsourcing companies.

author: Paul Tiyambe Zeleza
title: The Historiographical Legacy of B.A. Ogot and His Generation
content:
Good evening, colleagues, and the Governor of Kisumu County, Professor Anyang Nyong’o! It is truly a pleasure for me to join you in this commemoration of the towering historian, scholar, and public intellectual, Bethwell Alan Ogot. I believe I speak on behalf of all of us in extending our deep gratitude to the Council for the Development of Social Science Research in Africa (CODESRIA) and the Department of History at Kenyatta University for organizing this important conference. Personally, my appreciation extends to that rarity of experiences, the opportunity to meet several of my former students at Kenyatta University between 1984 and 1989 who have become distinguished academics and administrators. It’s a befitting tribute to our intellectual father, grandfather, quickly becoming a great-grandfather, who was raised and spent his last years and is buried in nearby Yala, that this conference is being held in his home city of Kisumu, under the transformative leadership of one of Kenya’s leading scholars and public intellectuals, Governor Peter Anyang Nyong’o.




Introduction




Let me begin by noting that I last visited Kisumu in January 2019 to join Professor Ogot as he celebrated his 90th birthday. author: Gboyega Ogundele
title: The Silk Drum
content:
Part One: The Arrival




In the year 1926, when the sun still climbed slow and steady over the red roofs of Ibadan, and the roads remained loyal to dust and earth, a man stepped off a creaking lorry with a chest of tea and a drum wrapped in silk. His name was Li Wei. His Mandarin name meant “strength and clarity,” but here in the sweltering market noise of a Yoruba town, names meant less than survival.




He stood still for a while, his pale robe gathering dirt around the hem, as he surveyed the open stalls, the scent of pepper and charcoal in the air, and the voices—singing, haggling, drumming—all clashing like waves. He had learned some English before the voyage but no Yoruba. Still, his father had said, “Listen first, then speak. The soul of trade is not in words but in silence and eyes.”




Li Wei rented a modest wooden stall at the edge of the market, shaded by an iroko tree. He unpacked the chests carefully. Inside were paper-tied bundles of oolong and pu-erh tea, dried hibiscus leaves, and a small red clay kettle. He placed the silk drum, still wrapped, beneath the table, away from sight.




 




Part Two: The Girl and the Drum




Adunni had always been drawn to rhythm. She did not speak it. She heard it. In the morning when the cock crowed, she listened to the way the sound bounced off the walls. When her mother pounded yam, Adunni matched the beat with her toes.

author: Frashia Muthoni Karanja
title: The Red Earth Between Us
content:
Before steel crossed Kimuka, morning arrived on bare soles pressing into the earth, you could hear the footsteps before you saw the people. The striking red volcanic soil, rich in iron oxides, would easily stick and cake sandals when wet. The visible stains on livestock, rusty-red taint would easily contrast with the green and dry-yellow grass of Kajiado plains. By evening it had climbed into socks, fingernails, cooking pots and mattresses.




Women woke first. Muthoni was up by the time roosters crowed. The cold had unsettled sleep, her mother was crouched beside the hearth, blowing gently into last night’s charcoal until the first orange glow returned. Smoke thickened beneath the low roof, stinging Muthoni’s eyes. Then the shifting would begin from the 

bomas,

 hooves scrapping, goats jostling inside a thorned fence. Across the ridge another woman was sweeping her compound with a twig broom. Her body was already answering an inherited clock that did not care for alarms. 




She tied her 

leso

, its fabric softened by years of washing, and stepped outside. The air smelled of smoke from last night’s fires, of damp grass, of goats shifting in their sleep. Somewhere, a rooster misjudged the hour. She balanced the yellow jerrycan on her hip and began the walk toward the borehole, joining other women. They greeted each other softly, voices low, conserving breath for the climb

author: Dilman Dila
title: The Song in a Teacup
content:
She ignored her father’s gift for thirty years. He offered it to her, wrapped in a box, at her graduation party, as she stood in front of strangers, holding a roll of paper that said she had a degree in something. Perhaps the paper had her name, Anyeri, or perhaps it was defaced with the name he gave her, Labeno. She had not opened it since the chancellor gave it to her five hours earlier, for she did not unroll toilet paper until she wanted to use it. A figment of her mother’s spirit haloed above her, giving the party a semblance of happiness, hugging her just as it had over the last many years. The only recognizable face in the tent was that of her littlest brother, Ocora, and she smiled at him for he had her mother’s face.




The tent stood uneasily in their front yard, after a storm earlier in the day had nearly uprooted it. The cheap decorations were reduced to strips of colored polyester wrapped on poles, fluttering in the breeze like rags. The ‘high table’ was soaked, and the red plastic flowers struggled to make it look chic. Whatever beauty the artist had intended to conjure in arranging them around the white cake was lost, for the cake resembled a mound of millet bread. But the faces in the tent did not mind. They showed all their teeth in happiness, for the smell of kongo brewing in a neighbor’s compound promised them a wild night. To warm up, they held little glass

author: Adaobi Rosemary Ogueli
title: Agaekwe Bound To A Price
content:
Chapter One




With both knees bent near the bathroom door, Agaekwe held a wooden brush in her right hand. Its bristles, scattered and weak, bore witness to years of service. She sprinkled more soapy water across the remains of the old, cemented floor and squatted once more to scrub the bathroom floor, 

shi shi shi

. She moved the brush in circular patterns as she scrubbed, stepping backward carefully with each stroke to avoid treading on the freshly cleaned surface. As the only girl in a family of five children, the burden of the Saturday clean-up fell largely on her, regardless of her brothers’ ages.




The street hummed with the noise of children queuing up at Mama Chidera’s shop for akara and akamu. In most African homes, this was the traditional Saturday meal: beans ground with a mortar and pestle until smooth, seasoned with onion, pepper, and crayfish, then molded by hand and dropped into hot oil until golden brown. Though akara was often seen as a staple for the poor due to its affordability, Mama Chidera’s was exceptional, stuffed with boiled eggs that only the middle class could truly afford.




No one detested akara; it might have seemed like food for the poor because it was very affordable, yet the rich equally queued for this particular akara ball. Mama Chidera added boiled eggs to hers, which made it exceptional, and only the middle class could afford to buy t

author: Kate Qiyu Chen
title: Teaching African Literature in a Small American Town
content:
1.




One week after returning to China for the summer, I came down with a cold and a fever.




During my recovery, I shut off every channel through which work could reach me, as though I were gradually drifting away from a particular identity and the time-space it inhabited. I watched Japanese anime and read Chinese books. For a while, my English and Kiswahili went to sleep. My e-reader, loaded with more than a dozen books for next semester’s research plans, had not been turned on for a week. It, too, lay quietly asleep.




On the first day after I recovered, with little to do—or perhaps nudged by preparations for next semester’s teaching—I returned to my summer reading: 

Nnedi Okorafor

‘s novel 

Lagoon

. Her leaping prose and fluid storytelling felt like seawater, like waves, and even more like the mist that, in the novel, hangs over Lagos. The book awakened my memories. It awakened another identity within me, along with the time-space in which it dwells.




2. 




“What is your research?”

“African literature.”




Just these two words—“Africa” and “literature”—are enough to trigger a cascade of questions.

author: Jude Chudi Okpala
title: Child of Mao
content:
Everything changed when she heard her parents speaking again in a language she could not understand. They had done that several times and often did so after raising their voices at each other in English. She had just come from Africa, where she believed she belonged even with the cut-eyes people showed her. They denied that she’s African because she had light skin and long hair, while everyone around her age was very dark and had low-cropped and abrasive hair. They did not know when she came to Africa because they started seeing her out of the blue, and she grew among them. Yet, they even coined the most mournful idea that anyone seen in the dark was not from Africa; and to that, they added that they did not know whom she looked like. Majority of them claimed she must look like her mother since they have never seen her and always pointed at the sizes of her eyes, nose, lips, and feet. At times, they wondered about what they said about her because she spoke their language very well, even with a flair. She could sing the folk songs and sort out the riddles. In their mind, though, they believed she was beautiful and dreamed of being like her. But they did not tell her. Her grandma, however, called her openly “

author: Aidan Huang
title: What Went Wrong in a Chinese-Run House in Chad
content:
From the airplane window, the land appeared almost uniformly yellow, stretched flat and uninterrupted beneath the wing. It was not the yellow of sunlight, but of dust and sand pressed into a vast plain, where roads were barely distinguishable from the earth around them. As the plane descended, the color did not change—it only grew closer. When the cabin door finally opened, heat rushed in immediately, dense and unapologetic, wrapping itself around the body before there was time to adjust. Outside, people moved through the glare wearing long sleeves, as if skin here had learned its own rules. Motorcycles dominated the roads, fast and loosely choreographed, riders weaving through traffic without helmets, without hesitation. Cars sped past on sand-colored streets, engines loud, windows open. I was driven through the city in a modest vehicle by a local professor—someone widely respected, I was later told—yet the ride itself felt precarious, carried forward by momentum more than by control. Only later did I begin to name the place where all of this was unfolding: N’Djamena, Chad.




Approaching N’Djamena from the air.




I had come here knowing that I would stay for two years. I was an early-career, female, Chinese researcher preparing for long-term fieldwork, and I arrived carrying not only academic plans but a quiet accumulation of unease. Before Chad, I had been based in North

author: Shams Wang Xin
title: Baptism by the Atlantic: Ethnographic Field Notes on Faith and Renjianshi of Chinese Migration in Cape Verde
content:
Praia, Santiago Island — Jan 1, 2025




[08:32 a.m]




The beach of São Francisco was half-empty when we arrived. The morning light had a metallic edge, slicing through the mist that hung low over the Atlantic. The beach smelled faintly of salt, diesel, and prayer. A speaker played a gospel hymn in Creole, punctuated by waves hitting the rocks.




A small crowd gathered near the shore. Three Chinese men stood apart from the rest, each holding a towel while wearing the pure white cloak. The pastors, two tall Cape Verdean men named João and Manuel, and an invited pastor from South Korea, smiled as they shook their hands. 




[08:50 a.m]




João lifted his Bible, the pages swollen with moisture. “Água é vida,” he said. Water is life. Then he continued, “And life is not divided by language.” That line stayed with me. Around us, Portuguese, Língua Kabuverdianu, Korean, and Mandarin drifted like separate waves, sometimes colliding, sometimes harmonizing.




The three Chinese men listened attentively. The man, Lin Yi, wore a long white cloak that fluttered in the wind. He had come from Wenzhou six months earlier to sell Chinese fried noodles and chicken in Praia’s market. “I didn’t come for baptism,” he told me quietly, “but maybe it came for me.”
